theme_measure_sec <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 10, base_family = "sans") +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),

## Scope

This vignette uses `sec_branched`, a synthetic dataset. Each sample has fixed
molecular weight, radius of gyration, and intrinsic viscosity values repeated
on its elution-time rows. The calculations below reduce those rows to one
record per sample before fitting or plotting.

The dataset includes a simulated MALS signal and supplied `rg` values. The
current `step_sec_mals()` implementation uses a single-angle approximation; it
does not fit multi-angle data or calculate radius of gyration. The examples
here pass the supplied `rg` and intrinsic-viscosity values to the branching
functions.

Branching indices compare a sample with a linear reference at matching
molecular weight. Estimates of branches per molecule also depend on the
architecture model supplied to the function.

## Data and sample-level properties

```{r setup}
library(measure)
library(measure.sec)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r data}
data(sec_branched, package = "measure.sec")

sample_properties <- sec_branched |>
  distinct(sample_id, topology, mw, branching_index, rg, intrinsic_visc) |>
  arrange(mw, topology)

sample_properties
```

The `branching_index` column is supplied with the example data. The next
section calculates the Rg-based index `g` from `rg` and an interpolated linear
reference. These are separate quantities: `g` uses radius of gyration, while
the supplied index is based on intrinsic viscosity.

## Rg-based branching index

For a sample and linear reference at the same molecular weight,
`measure_branching_index()` calculates

$$g = \frac{R_g^2(\text{sample})}{R_g^2(\text{linear reference})}.$$

A value below 1 means the sample has a smaller radius of gyration than the
reference at that molecular weight. The interpretation depends on the quality
and range of the reference data; this example uses only the three supplied
linear reference values.

```{r branching-index}
linear_ref <- sample_properties |>
  filter(topology == "linear") |>
  select(mw, rg) |>
  arrange(mw)

branch100 <- sample_properties |>
  filter(sample_id == "Branch-100K")

g_result <- measure_branching_index(
  mw = branch100$mw,
  rg = branch100$rg,
  reference = linear_ref,
  method = "g"
)

print(g_result)

branching_results <- sample_properties |>
  mutate(
    g = vapply(
      seq_len(nrow(sample_properties)),
      function(i) {
        measure_branching_index(
          mw = sample_properties$mw[i],
          rg = sample_properties$rg[i],
          reference = linear_ref,
          method = "g"
        )$g[[1]]
      },
      numeric(1)
    )
  )

branching_results
```

```{r g-by-mw, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Rg-based branching index calculated from the synthetic sample-level properties and the supplied linear reference. The dashed line marks g = 1, the linear-reference value.", fig.alt = "Scatter chart of molecular weight in Da versus the Rg-based branching index g for synthetic linear, branched, and star samples. Linear samples are at g = 1 at 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 Da; the branched samples range from about 0.54 to 0.68, and the two star samples are about 0.39 and 0.47. The dashed horizontal line marks g = 1."}
ggplot(
  branching_results,
  aes(x = mw, y = g, colour = topology, shape = topology)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(aes(group = topology), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(linear = "#2E86AB", branched = "#A23B72", star = "#3B7A57")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Molecular weight (Da)",
    y = "Rg-based branching index, g",
    colour = "Topology",
    shape = "Topology"
  ) +
  theme_measure_sec()
```

## Branch-count estimates depend on architecture

`measure_branching_frequency()` maps `g` to branches per molecule under a
specified architecture. Here, the same `g` value from `Branch-100K` is passed
to four models. The results are model-dependent estimates, not direct counts
of branch points.

```{r branching-frequency}
g_for_frequency <- g_result$g[[1]]
architectures <- c("random", "star_3", "star_4", "comb")

frequency_results <- tibble::tibble(
  architecture = architectures,
  branches_per_molecule = vapply(
    architectures,
    function(architecture) {
      measure_branching_frequency(
        g = g_for_frequency,
        architecture = architecture
      )$branches_per_molecule[[1]]
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)

frequency_results
```

```{r architecture-estimates, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Branch-count estimates for the Branch-100K g value under four architecture assumptions. Each bar is the result returned by `measure_branching_frequency()` for that model.", fig.alt = "Bar chart of estimated branches per molecule for the same synthetic Branch-100K g value, about 0.63. The random model returns about 7.7, the star_3 and star_4 models return 1 each, and the comb model returns about 0.9."}
ggplot(
  frequency_results,
  aes(x = architecture, y = branches_per_molecule)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "#2E86AB") +
  labs(
    x = "Assumed architecture",
    y = "Estimated branches per molecule"
  ) +
  theme_measure_sec()
```

## Mark-Houwink relationship

The Mark-Houwink equation relates intrinsic viscosity to molecular weight:

$$[\eta] = K M^a.$$

The exponent depends on the polymer, solvent, temperature, and molecular-weight
range. The points below use the sample-level values in the synthetic dataset;
lines are descriptive log-log fits for the linear and branched samples.

```{r mark-houwink}
linear_data <- sample_properties |>
  filter(topology == "linear", intrinsic_visc > 0)

mh <- measure_mh_parameters(
  mw = linear_data$mw,
  intrinsic_visc = linear_data$intrinsic_visc
)

print(mh)

mh_comparison <- sample_properties |>
  filter(topology %in% c("linear", "branched"))
```

```{r mh-comparison, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Sample-level intrinsic viscosity values and log-log linear fits for the supplied linear and branched examples. Each point is one distinct sample, not one elution-time row.", fig.alt = "Log-log scatter chart of molecular weight in Da versus intrinsic viscosity in mL/g for synthetic linear and branched samples. At each of 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 Da, the linear sample has higher intrinsic viscosity than the branched sample. Solid fitted lines are drawn separately for the two topologies."}
ggplot(
  mh_comparison,
  aes(x = mw, y = intrinsic_visc, colour = topology, shape = topology)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(linear = "#2E86AB", branched = "#A23B72")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Molecular weight (Da)",
    y = "Intrinsic viscosity (mL/g)",
    colour = "Topology",
    shape = "Topology"
  ) +
  theme_measure_sec()
```

## Radius-of-gyration scaling

`measure_rg_mw_scaling()` fits the supplied linear-reference values. The fitted
slope summarizes this three-point synthetic example; it is not a validated
polymer or solvent parameter.

```{r rg-scaling}
rg_scaling <- measure_rg_mw_scaling(
  mw = linear_data$mw,
  rg = linear_data$rg
)

print(rg_scaling)
```

`plot_sec_conformation()` can show the log-log relationships and fitted slopes
for each topology. Its slope labels summarize the values provided in
`sec_branched`.

```{r conformation-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Log-log relationship between molecular weight and radius of gyration for the synthetic samples. Dashed lines and slope labels summarize a separate fit for each topology.", fig.alt = "Scatter chart of log10 molecular weight in Da versus log10 radius of gyration in nm for synthetic linear, branched, and star samples. Each group has a dashed fitted line and a slope label; the star group contains two points and the other groups contain three."}
plot_sec_conformation(
  sample_properties,
  type = "rg_mw",
  mw_col = "mw",
  y_col = "rg",
  sample_id = "topology",
  show_fit = TRUE,
  show_exponent = TRUE
) +
  labs(
    x = "log10 molecular weight (Da)",
    y = "log10 radius of gyration (nm)"
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(label = ""))) +
  theme_measure_sec()
```

## Comparing branching models

`measure_branching_model_comparison()` also compares the Rg-based values with
model predictions. The input uses one value per branched sample.

```{r model-comparison}
branched_results <- branching_results |>
  filter(topology == "branched")

model_comparison <- measure_branching_model_comparison(
  g = branched_results$g,
  mw = branched_results$mw
)

print(model_comparison)
```
